title: Sammy Hopes India Series Showing Helps West Indies Attract Sponsors and Financial Backing
excerpt: West Indies drew the five-match T20I series 2-2 in India after rain washed out the Bengaluru decider, and head coach Daren Sammy said the performance should put his financially strained team 'in a conversation' for support.
body:
• West Indies head coach Daren Sammy said he hopes his team's 2-2 T20I series draw in India helps West Indies cricket attract sponsors and financial backing.
  • The five-match series ended 2-2 after rain washed out the decider in Bengaluru on October 17, with India 118 for 5 in 7.4 overs in a match reduced to nine overs a side.
  • Sammy called the result a "massive step" against the defending champions in their own backyard, and said the team's "swagger is back."
  • Cricket West Indies announced financial restructuring last month, including a 25% pay cut for contracted international players, according to ESPNcricinfo.

West Indies head coach Daren Sammy has said he hopes his team's performance in India helps West Indies cricket attract the sponsors and financial backing it needs, after the five-match T20I series ended drawn 2-2. Speaking after rain washed out the deciding fifth match in Bengaluru, Sammy framed the on-field result as a commercial argument: a competitive West Indies side, performing against India in India, is a product sponsors can buy into.

A drawn series, decided by rain

The series decider at the M. Chinnaswamy Stadium on Saturday, October 17 never produced a result. IANS reports persistent drizzle delayed the toss, the match was reduced to nine overs a side with a 9:15 pm start, and India reached 118 for 5 in 7.4 overs before heavier rain forced the covers on. The match was abandoned at 10:16 pm, with no possibility of a five-over West Indies chase of 84 before the 10:21 pm cut-off. Ishan Kishan made 30 off 10 balls and Naman Dhir an unbeaten 24 off six; Shamar Springer took 2 for 17 and Keemo Paul 2 for 34.

The washout denied West Indies a chance at their first series win in India since 2002, IANS noted. It also closed the stadium's first international fixture in two years without a finish, after the crowd had waited through hours of rain.

"The swagger is back"

Sammy treated 2-2 as a fair result and a breakthrough in context. West Indies had lost all three of their previous bilateral T20I series in India, winning one match out of seven across them, ESPNcricinfo reports. This time they matched the defending T20 champions across four completed matches.

"We played against the defending champions and we've matched them, and in certain areas we've outplayed them, especially in their backyard."

— Daren Sammy, West Indies head coach

"It's a true reflection of how all the teams have played, especially for our guys," Sammy said at the post-match press conference. "I'm pretty sure when the series started, we probably didn't have a chance. But that was just the opinion of others." He added that West Indies would have wanted the win, "because something we've not done forever in India," and pointed to the home leg win in 2023, when West Indies beat India 3-2. "All the guys in the dressing room, they've gone out there and played with intent," he said. "The swagger is back, the confidence is back."

The draw follows a T20I series win over Sri Lanka at home and a semi-final finish at the 2026 T20 World Cup in India in March, per ESPNcricinfo.

The finances behind the comments

Sammy's sponsorship hope sits against a hard financial backdrop. ESPNcricinfo reports that Cricket West Indies announced major financial restructuring last month, including a 25% pay cut for contracted international players. Sammy linked the instability to a structural change dating to 1997, when, according to CWI chief executive Chris Dehring, the ICC voted to change international cricket's financial model so host boards kept all revenue from bilateral series. The loss of touring fees removed a key source of stability for boards representing smaller populations, such as the West Indies, and West Indies cricket has faced repeated financial crises since.

"We're in a position where we need somebody to put a hand around the shoulder of West Indies cricket. Financially, that is, and series like this, here in India, against the best team in the world, puts us in a conversation closer to that."

— Daren Sammy, West Indies head coach

Sammy also invoked the commercial footprint of past West Indies teams, who spent months on tour playing warm-up matches, built fan bases and generated revenue wherever they played. His argument to sponsors and administrators was direct: West Indies cricket means a great deal "not only to the region but to the world and to the game," and performances like this series are the evidence. For Indian audiences, the series delivered a competitive contest against a storied opponent; for West Indies cricket, Sammy is asking whether that attention can now be converted into the backing that keeps the team competitive.
